extracted.intended_audience: general readers, students and researchers interested in British comedy and its history
extracted.subtask_description: An encyclopedic overview of the history, media formats, recurring features, and notable practitioners of comedy in Britain, describing how different forms (theatre, radio, television) and subgenres (satire, pantomime, alternative comedy) developed and interrelate.

rubrics_metrics.name: Satire
rubrics_metrics.description: Satire has been a major feature of comedy in the British Isles for centuries.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The article cites pictorial satire (William Hogarth) and political cartoons (James Gillray) as precursors; later examples include TV satirical series like That Was The Week That Was, Not the Nine O'Clock News, and the puppet satire Spitting Image. Satire often targets politics, entertainment, sport, and culture.

rubrics_metrics.name: Pantomime and slapstick tradition
rubrics_metrics.description: In early 19th-century Britain, pantomime acquired its present form, which includes slapstick comedy and featured the first mainstream clown, Joseph Grimaldi.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Pantomime and physical slapstick shaped performance skills used by later comedians; music hall and pantomime produced performers such as Charlie Chaplin, Stan Laurel, George Formby, and Dan Leno.

rubrics_metrics.name: Radio comedy / BBC dominance
rubrics_metrics.description: Radio comedy in Britain has been almost exclusively the preserve of the BBC.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: 1940s–50s variety programmes dominated (e.g., It's That Man Again, Much Binding in the Marsh). Notable radio series include Hancock's Half Hour and Round the Horne; later radio embraced panel game formats like Just a Minute, I'm Sorry I Haven't a Clue, and The News Quiz. Some radio shows transferred to television.

rubrics_metrics.name: Sketch comedy (including dialogue-free sketches)
rubrics_metrics.description: Sketch shows and short-form sketches are a recurring format; Fred Karno developed a form of sketch comedy without dialogue in the 1890s.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Dialogue-free visual sketches influenced performers such as Chaplin and Laurel; sketch shows have remained a staple of British comedy on radio and television.

rubrics_metrics.name: Sitcoms as television staple
rubrics_metrics.description: Following the success of Hancock's Half Hour and Steptoe and Son, sitcoms became a part of some television schedules.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The BBC has generally been dominant in television comedy, though commercial stations have had successes. Sitcoms sit alongside other television formats such as sketch shows and panel programmes.

rubrics_metrics.name: Variety of television formats (stand-up, impressionists, puppet shows)
rubrics_metrics.description: Television comedy in Britain encompasses multiple formats including sketch shows, stand-up comedy, impressionists, and puppet shows.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples include satirical puppet show Spitting Image and various stand-up and impressionist programmes; different formats allow different comic techniques (e.g., character work, impersonation, topical satire).

rubrics_metrics.name: Panel games and satire crossover
rubrics_metrics.description: British satire has also gone over into quiz and panel shows.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Shows such as Have I Got News for You, 8 out of 10 Cats, and Shooting Stars illustrate how quiz/panel formats are used for topical and satirical comedy.

rubrics_metrics.name: Alternative comedy characteristics
rubrics_metrics.description: Alternative comedy, spearheaded in the 1980s by figures such as Ben Elton and The Comic Strip, employed new approaches and sensibilities.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Key features include a break from traditional music-hall/variety forms, and later practitioners used editing, surreal humour, and cultural references (1990s–2000s) to achieve effect. Notable performers include Alexei Sayle, Rik Mayall, and French and Saunders.

rubrics_metrics.name: Long historical continuity and roots
rubrics_metrics.description: British comedy history is measured in centuries, with roots in Shakespearean stage comedy, Punch and Judy puppet shows, music hall, and 18th–19th century pictorial satire.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: Shakespeare's use of chase scenes and beatings (The Comedy of Errors), first recorded Punch and Judy in 1662 (Samuel Pepys), and 18th-century political cartooning; these traditions influenced later forms and performers.
